journeyIntro: For making and keeping meaningful friendships. Learn to listen, show up and navigate changing needs.

lessons.title: Reach Out First
lessons.summary: Friendship grows through small invitations.

steps.title: Someone has to go first
steps.body: Many friendships fade not because anyone stopped caring, but because both people waited for the other to get in touch. Going first is a gift.

steps.prompt: You haven’t seen a good friend for months and you miss them. What’s the best next step?

options.text: Wait for them to message first this time.
options.why: If they’re waiting too, the silence just keeps growing on both sides.

options.text: “I’ve missed you! Fancy a coffee next week?”
options.why: It’s warm, specific and easy to say yes to, with no blame about the gap.

options.text: “You never get in touch any more.”
options.why: Opening with blame can make them feel guilty rather than glad to hear from you.

steps.prompt: Make the invitation easy.
steps.before: I’ve missed you! Are you free for
steps.why: A small, low-pressure plan is easy to fit in, which makes a yes much more likely.

steps.prompt: What stops you reaching out to friends first?
steps.reply: Totally understandable. Most people are simply glad to be thought of.

steps.title: An old friend is back

lines.text: Guess who’s moved back to town for good! 🎉
Honestly, I barely know anyone here any more 😅

steps.prompt: What do you send back?

options.text: Nice! We should hang out sometime.
options.why: “Sometime” rarely turns into a plan, so they may stay just as lonely as before.

options.text: Oh cool, have fun settling in!
options.why: Friendly, but it misses the hint that they’d love some company.

options.text: Welcome back! Dinner this week? Thursday works for me.
options.why: You heard the hint and made a specific, easy plan, which is exactly how friendships restart.

steps.body: Send one warm, low-pressure invitation today to a friend you haven’t seen for a while.

lessons.title: Make Plans Happen
lessons.summary: Turn “we should hang out” into a real date.

steps.title: “Sometime” rarely comes
steps.body: “We should catch up sometime!” feels friendly, but without a day and a place it usually drifts away. The friend who names a time is the one who makes it happen.

steps.prompt: You bump into a friend in the supermarket and you both say you should catch up. What makes it actually happen?

options.text: “Are you free Saturday morning? There’s a new café by the park.”
options.why: A specific day and place turns a nice idea into a plan they can say yes to.

options.text: “Let’s definitely do something soon!”
options.why: It sounds keen, but “soon” has no date, so it easily slips.

options.text: Wait and see if they message you about it.
options.why: If you both wait, the good intention fades away.

steps.prompt: Make it concrete.
steps.why: Naming a real day gives the plan a place in both your diaries.

steps.prompt: Who have you said “we should catch up” to lately?
steps.reply: One quick message with a day in it could turn that into a real plan.

steps.prompt: A real plan or a vague one?

cards.text: “Drinks at the Fox, Friday at seven?”
Sending a calendar invite after you agree

steps.why: Real plans have a when and a where. Vague ones leave all the work to the other person, so they rarely happen.

steps.body: Turn one “we should catch up” into a real plan today, with a day, a time and a place.

lessons.title: Make New Friends
lessons.summary: Grown-up friendships start with small, repeated hellos.

steps.title: Friendship grows from repeat contact
steps.body: Most adult friendships start with someone you keep seeing: a colleague, a gym regular, a parent at the school gate. A little more chat each time is how strangers become friends.

steps.prompt: You’ve chatted with someone at your climbing class a few times and you get on well. What’s a natural next step?

options.text: Ask them to be your new best friend.
options.why: Too much, too soon can feel like pressure, even if it’s meant kindly.

options.text: Keep chatting at class and hope it grows on its own.
options.why: Friendly, but without an invite it may stay a class-only chat forever.

options.text: “A few of us get food after class on Thursday. Want to come?”
options.why: A light, low-stakes invite gives the friendship a chance to grow beyond class.

steps.prompt: A low-pressure invite.
steps.before: We’re grabbing a coffee after this, you’re
steps.why: “Welcome” makes it an open door, not an obligation, so it’s easy to say yes or no.

steps.prompt: Where could you meet new friends right now?
steps.reply: Places you go regularly are the best soil for new friendships to grow.

steps.prompt: From stranger to friend. Put these in order.
items: Say hello and learn their name
steps.why: Friendships build in small steps. Each one makes the next feel natural rather than forced.

steps.body: Learn the name of someone you see often, or take one chat a step further today.

lessons.title: Be Present
lessons.summary: Let a friend finish their story.

steps.title: The gift of full attention
steps.body: In a world of buzzing phones, simply listening to a friend without interrupting is rare. It tells them, more than words can, that they matter.

steps.prompt: Over coffee, a friend starts telling you about a really disappointing weekend. What’s the best response?

options.text: “Mine was even worse, listen to this.”
options.why: Swapping in your story moves the spotlight away just as they were opening up.

options.text: “Oh no, that sounds rough. What happened?”
options.why: It acknowledges the disappointment and invites the full story, so they feel heard.

options.text: “Look on the bright side, at least it’s Monday!”
options.why: Quick cheer-ups can feel like being hurried past a feeling they wanted to share.

steps.title: Let them finish
steps.body: Resist the urge to jump in with advice or your own story. Ask one more question than feels natural; friends often save the real part for last.

steps.prompt: Keep the story going.
steps.why: An open question keeps them talking and shows you’re interested in all of it.

steps.prompt: What makes it hardest to stay present when a friend talks?
steps.reply: Noticing it is the first step. Gently bring your attention back when you catch it.

steps.prompt: Present or distracted?

cards.text: Checking a text halfway through their story
Planning your reply while they talk

steps.why: Being present is mostly about small signals: eyes up, phone away and questions that follow their thread.

steps.body: Next time a friend shares something, give them two full minutes of attention before you say anything about yourself.

lessons.title: Ask Better Questions
lessons.summary: Good questions show you want the real answer.

steps.title: Questions that open doors
steps.body: “How are you?” usually gets “fine”. Questions about something specific, like the trip they mentioned or the new job, invite a real story instead of a polite reply.

steps.prompt: Your friend has just started a new job. Which question is most likely to start a real conversation?

options.text: “Job going okay?”
options.why: It’s easy to answer with one word, so the chat may stop there.

options.text: “What’s surprised you most in your first week?”
options.why: It’s specific and open, so they can share a real moment rather than a quick update.

options.text: “Is it better than your last place?”
options.why: It invites a quick comparison rather than their actual experience.

steps.prompt: Keep their story going.
steps.why: A simple follow-up shows you’re with them and want to hear the rest.

steps.prompt: Which question do you rely on too often?
steps.reply: Swapping in one specific question can make the same catch-up feel much closer.

steps.prompt: Match each quick question with a better one.
steps.why: Better questions are specific and open. They show you remember their life and want more than a one-word answer.

steps.body: Next time you see a friend, swap “How are you?” for one specific question about their life.

lessons.title: Remember the Details
lessons.summary: Small follow-ups say “I was really listening”.

steps.title: Details are a quiet kind of care
steps.body: When you remember their interview, their dog’s name or the date of their exam, it shows they matter to you. A quick “How did it go?” can mean more than a big gesture.

steps.prompt: Last week a friend mentioned their driving test was on Tuesday. It’s now Wednesday. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for them to bring it up.
options.why: They may not want to announce it, especially if it went badly.

options.text: Ask about it next time you happen to see them.
options.why: Kind, but by then the moment may have passed.

options.text: “Thinking of you! How did the driving test go yesterday?”
options.why: A timely message shows you remembered and care how it went, pass or fail.

steps.prompt: A simple memory trick.
steps.before: When a friend mentions a big day, put a
steps.why: You don’t need a perfect memory. A quick reminder lets you show up at the right moment.

steps.prompt: What’s coming up for a friend soon that you could check in about?

steps.title: The day after

lines.text: How did the big presentation go yesterday? 🤞
Omg you remembered!! It went really well actually

steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: Nice 👍
options.why: A quick reply is fine, but it closes the door just as they were about to share.

options.text: Yay!! Tell me everything, what was the best moment? 🎉
options.reaction: Okay so my boss actually clapped 😂
options.why: You celebrate with them and invite the story, which makes the check-in feel special.

options.text: Told you it would be fine. Anyway, guess what happened to me…
options.why: Switching to your news takes the moment away from them.

steps.body: Set one reminder to check in on a friend’s upcoming big day, then send the message.

lessons.title: Say What Matters
lessons.summary: Speak honestly without making accusations.

steps.title: Unsaid things grow
steps.body: When a friend keeps doing something that hurts, staying quiet can feel kinder. But small hurts that go unsaid often quietly end friendships.

steps.prompt: A friend has cancelled on you at the last minute three times this month. What do you say?

options.text: “I feel let down when plans change last minute. Can we plan something that suits you?”
options.why: It’s honest about the impact and moves towards a solution, not a verdict on them.

options.text: “Honestly, you’re a terrible friend.”
options.why: A label hurts and gets them defending themselves, so the real issue gets lost.

options.text: Say nothing and quietly stop inviting them.
options.why: They may never know why things changed, and you lose a friendship that could be saved.

steps.title: Feeling, then request
steps.body: Share how it felt, then what would help: “I was disappointed when Friday fell through. Could we pick a time that works better for you?”

steps.prompt: Share the feeling.
steps.why: Naming your feeling honestly gives them a chance to understand and make it right.

steps.prompt: Is there something you’ve been wanting to say to a friend? How could you put it?
Match each accusation with a fairer way to say it.

pairs.b: “I’d love to share my news too.”
“Can we pick a time that works?”

steps.why: Each rewrite swaps a label for a feeling or a request, which is much easier for a friend to hear and act on.

steps.body: Share one honest feeling with a friend, followed by a practical request, rather than letting it build up.

lessons.title: Raise Things Early
lessons.summary: Small niggles are easier to fix while they’re small.

steps.title: Niggles grow in the dark
steps.body: A friend who’s always late, or always picks the restaurant, can start to grate. Left unsaid, small things pile up until they burst out at the wrong moment.

steps.prompt: Your friend has been 30 minutes late to the last three meet-ups. It’s starting to bother you. What’s best?

options.text: Say nothing. It’s only a small thing.
options.why: Small things that keep happening tend to grow into resentment.

options.text: “I love our catch-ups. Lately I’ve been waiting a while, could we aim for on time?”
options.why: Warm, early and specific. It names the pattern without making them the villain.

options.text: Start turning up late yourself so they see how it feels.
options.why: Tit-for-tat makes things worse and they may not even notice why.

steps.prompt: The best time to raise it.
steps.before: It’s easiest to bring something up while it’s still
steps.why: Early on, it’s a quick chat. Months later, it can feel like an accusation.

steps.prompt: Is there a small thing you’ve been sitting on with a friend?
steps.reply: Raising it gently now protects the friendship from a bigger blow-up later.

steps.prompt: Raising it early, or letting it build?

cards.text: Mentioning it the first time it really bugs you
Keeping a mental list of every time
Exploding about it a year later

steps.why: Raising things early keeps them small and fixable. Letting them build turns a niggle into a real rift.

steps.body: If something small has been bugging you with a friend, mention it kindly this week while it’s still small.

lessons.title: Kind Honesty
lessons.summary: Be honest when asked, and kind in how you say it.

steps.title: Honest and kind can go together
steps.body: When a friend asks what you really think, empty praise doesn’t help them, and blunt criticism hurts. Start with what’s good, be clear about your concern, and leave the choice with them.

steps.prompt: Your friend shows you a long, angry text they plan to send their landlord, and asks what you think. It could backfire. What do you say?

options.text: “Looks great, send it!”
options.why: It avoids awkwardness now, but they may pay for it later.

options.text: “That’s a terrible idea.”
options.why: Honest, but so blunt they may feel judged and stop listening.

options.text: “You’re right to be annoyed. I worry the tone could backfire. Tweak it together?”
options.why: You back their feelings, share an honest concern and offer help, while the choice stays theirs.

steps.prompt: Leave the decision with them.
steps.before: That’s my honest view, but it’s
steps.why: Honesty lands better when they know you respect their right to decide.

steps.prompt: When a friend asks for your opinion, you tend to…
options: Say what they want to hear
steps.reply: Knowing your habit helps you aim for the sweet spot: kind and honest at once.

steps.prompt: Match each blunt line with a kinder honest one.

pairs.b: “I worry about how he treats you.”

steps.why: Kind honesty says the true thing in a way the other person can actually hear and use.

steps.body: Next time a friend asks your opinion, start with something genuine you like, then share one honest concern.

lessons.title: Tone in Texts
lessons.summary: Messages lose your voice, so add it back in.

steps.title: Texts lose your tone of voice
steps.body: Face to face, your smile softens “Fine.” In a text, it can read as cold. Short replies, missing emojis and late-night messages are easy to misread, both ways.

steps.prompt: A friend asks if you mind them bringing their new partner to your birthday drinks. You don’t mind at all. What do you send?

options.text: “Fine.”
options.why: You mean it kindly, but on screen it can read as annoyed.

options.text: “Of course! Can’t wait to meet them 😊”
options.why: Warm words and a little emoji make your real tone clear.
Very easy to read as irritated or uninterested.

steps.prompt: Check before you assume.
steps.before: If a message feels off, ask before you
steps.why: Many “rude” texts were just rushed. A quick check saves a lot of hurt.

steps.prompt: Which texting habit causes you the most mix-ups?
steps.reply: Small tweaks, like a warmer word or a quick check-in, prevent a lot of misunderstandings.

steps.title: A short reply

lines.text: So sorry, I have to cancel tonight 😩 Work disaster.

steps.prompt: It feels cold. What do you do?

options.text: Assume they’re furious and stew on it.
options.why: Guessing the worst from one word can create a problem that isn’t there.

options.text: Reply “Wow, okay then.”
options.why: Reacting to the tone you imagined can start a real argument.

options.text: “I hate cancelling on you. Are you okay? Can we do Saturday instead?”
options.reaction: Sorry, was just busy! Saturday’s great 💛
options.why: You checked in warmly instead of assuming, and offered a new plan.

steps.body: Before you send your next few texts, reread them once and ask: could this sound colder than I mean?

lessons.title: Keep Healthy Space
lessons.summary: Good friends can have different capacities.

steps.title: Always-on isn’t a duty
steps.body: Group chats and instant messages can make it feel like you owe friends constant availability. Healthy friendships have room for rest.

steps.prompt: It’s late, you’re exhausted, and a friend keeps messaging about their dating drama. What do you do?

options.text: Keep replying until 2am out of guilt.
options.why: You’ll be drained tomorrow, and tired replies help them less than a fresh conversation.

options.text: Mute them for good without saying anything.
options.why: Going silent without a word can feel like rejection and confuse the friendship.

options.text: “I’m wiped out and logging off. Tell me everything tomorrow?”
options.why: It’s honest about your limit and shows you still care about what they’re going through.

steps.prompt: Set a kind limit.
steps.before: I need to sleep now, but
steps.why: Pairing your limit with a plan to reconnect keeps the care obvious.

steps.prompt: Where do you most need space from friends?
steps.reply: Good to know. A small, kind limit there protects both your energy and the friendship.

steps.title: A big favour

lines.text: Huge favour… can you help me move flat on Saturday? 🙏
It’ll take all day, and you’re the only one with a car.

steps.prompt: Saturday is your only free day. Reply:

options.text: I can’t do all day, but I can drive the big stuff from 10 till 12. Would that help?
options.reaction: That would be amazing, thank you!
options.why: You offer real help within a limit you can keep, so you stay generous without burning out.

options.text: Ugh, fine. I’ll be there.
options.why: A reluctant yes often turns into resentment, and they won’t know you were stretched.

options.text: Sorry, I’m busy that day.
options.why: It isn’t quite true, and they lose help you could have given in a smaller way.

steps.body: Set one kind limit around your availability this week, and say when you’ll be around instead.

lessons.title: Say No to a Friend
lessons.summary: A kind no keeps you a good friend, not a tired one.

steps.title: Saying no can protect the friendship
steps.body: If you say yes to everything, you end up tired and quietly resentful. A warm, clear no lets your yeses be real, and good friends can handle hearing it.

steps.prompt: A friend asks you to come to their cousin’s karaoke night. You’re exhausted and really don’t want to go. What’s best?

options.text: “Thanks for asking! I’m wiped this week, so I’ll pass, but have the best time 🎤”
options.why: Warm, honest and clear, with no need for a long excuse.

options.text: Say yes, then cancel at the last minute.
options.why: A late cancel feels worse to them than an honest no up front.

options.text: Invent a family emergency.
options.why: Made-up excuses can come back to bite and chip away at trust.

steps.prompt: Keep the no short.
steps.why: A short, kind no is clearer and easier to accept than a pile of excuses.

steps.prompt: What makes it hardest to say no to a friend?
steps.reply: Those feelings are normal. A kind no rarely costs a good friendship.

steps.prompt: A kind no, or an unkind one?

cards.text: “I can’t this time, but thanks for thinking of me.”
“Not for me, but I’d love to do dinner soon.”
“Ugh, why would I want to do that?”
A vague “maybe” you know is a no

steps.why: A kind no is clear and warm. Ignoring, mocking or a false maybe leaves them confused or hurt.

steps.body: The next time you don’t want to do something, try a short, warm no without a long excuse.

lessons.title: Different Paces
lessons.summary: Friends can reply, plan and share at different speeds.

steps.title: Not everyone texts like you
steps.body: Some friends reply in seconds; others take days. Some want weekly plans; others are happy with monthly. Different paces aren’t a sign someone cares less.

steps.prompt: Your friend often takes two or three days to reply, while you reply quickly. What’s the healthiest view?

options.text: They clearly don’t value me.
options.why: Slow replies usually reflect their habits, not how much they care.

options.text: Send follow-ups until they answer.
options.why: Chasing can feel like pressure and make replying feel like a chore.

options.text: “That’s just their rhythm. If it matters, I’ll ask what works for us.”
options.why: You accept their pace and stay free to talk about it if it starts to bother you.

steps.prompt: Talk about it openly.
steps.why: Agreeing how to reach each other for urgent things takes the pressure off everyday messages.

steps.prompt: What’s your natural friendship pace?
steps.reply: Knowing your own pace helps you see that a friend’s different rhythm isn’t a rejection.

steps.prompt: Match each difference with a fair middle ground.

pairs.a: They need lots of alone time

steps.why: Different paces work when you find a rhythm that fits you both, rather than asking one person to change completely.

steps.body: Think of a friend whose pace differs from yours, and let go of one story you’ve been telling about it.

lessons.title: Lending and Favours
lessons.summary: Help in ways you can give freely.

steps.title: Give what you can give freely
steps.body: Money and big favours can strain friendships. A useful rule: only lend what you could afford to lose, and only offer help you won’t resent giving.

steps.prompt: A friend asks to borrow a big sum until payday. You could lend a third of it without worry, but no more. What do you say?

options.text: Lend the full amount and hope it comes back.
options.why: If it’s late, the worry could turn into resentment.

options.text: “I can’t lend all of it, but I could lend a third. Would that help?”
options.why: You help within your limit and are clear about it, which protects the friendship.

options.text: Tell them you’re broke when you’re not.
options.why: A small lie can feel easier, but it adds distance and guilt.

steps.prompt: A good lending rule.
steps.before: Only lend what you could afford to
steps.why: Then if it comes back late, or not at all, the friendship survives.

steps.prompt: Has lending or a big favour ever strained a friendship of yours?
steps.reply: Many people have been there. Clear, kind limits help stop it happening again.

steps.prompt: Before saying yes to a big ask. Put these in order.
items: Check what you can truly give
steps.why: A pause stops an automatic yes; being clear about limits and details keeps everyone on the same page.

steps.body: Next time a friend asks a big favour, take a moment to decide what you can truly give before answering.

lessons.title: Follow Through
lessons.summary: Reliability is a quiet form of care.

steps.title: Showing up says a lot
steps.body: Turning up to the birthday, the gig, the hospital visit: these are the moments friends remember. Reliability quietly says, “You can count on me.”

steps.prompt: You said you’d come to your friend’s small art exhibition on Saturday. What’s the best way to handle it?

options.text: Forget, and hope they don’t notice you weren’t there.
options.why: They probably will notice, especially at a small event that means a lot to them.

options.text: Say “definitely!” without checking your plans.
options.why: Easy yeses that fall through hurt more than an honest “I’ll try, I’ll confirm Friday.”

options.text: Put it in your calendar now, and tell them early if anything changes.
options.why: Planning ahead makes it likely you’ll go, and an early heads-up respects their feelings.

steps.prompt: Be honest about plans.
steps.before: I’ve put it in my calendar, and I’ll
steps.why: An early heads-up gives them time to adjust and shows you take the plan seriously.

steps.prompt: When do you find it hardest to follow through for friends?
steps.reply: Knowing that helps you say yes more carefully, so your yeses can be trusted.

steps.prompt: A plan might fall through. Put these in order.
steps.why: Spotting it early and telling them quickly gives them time to adjust; a new time shows you still want to see them.

steps.body: Keep one promise to a friend this week, or let them know early and honestly if you can’t.

lessons.title: Keep Their Secrets
lessons.summary: What they share with you stays with you.

steps.title: Trust lives in what you don’t say
steps.body: When a friend tells you something private, they hand you a bit of their trust. Passing it on, even casually or to “just one person”, can break it fast.

steps.prompt: Your friend told you they’re thinking of leaving their job. A mutual friend asks, “Is something up with Alex?” What do you say?

options.text: “That’s Alex’s news to share. You could ask them!”
options.why: You stay friendly with both, without passing on what you were trusted with.

options.text: “Don’t say I told you, but they’re quitting.”
options.why: “Don’t say I told you” still breaks the trust.

options.text: “Nothing at all!”
options.why: Lying outright can backfire when the news comes out.

steps.prompt: When unsure, ask.
steps.before: Is this okay to share, or should I keep it
steps.why: If you’re not sure, a quick check shows care and avoids an accidental slip.

steps.prompt: When is it hardest to keep something to yourself?
steps.reply: Noticing your weak spot makes it much easier to pause before you share.

steps.prompt: Keeping trust, or breaking it?
steps.why: Even small hints or “in confidence” retellings pass on what wasn’t yours to share.

steps.body: If a friend has shared something private with you, quietly decide now that it stays with you.

lessons.title: Show Up When It’s Hard
lessons.summary: Reliability matters most on a friend’s worst days.

steps.title: Hard times show who’s there
steps.body: When a friend is ill, grieving or struggling, many people pull back because they don’t know what to say. Simply showing up, imperfectly, is what they remember.

steps.prompt: A friend has been off work for weeks with depression and has gone quiet. What helps most?

options.text: Give them space until they’re better.
options.why: Space can feel like being forgotten when someone is struggling.

options.text: Send a long message about how to feel better.
options.why: Advice can feel like pressure when they have little energy.

options.text: “Thinking of you. No need to reply. Can I drop round some food Thursday?”
options.why: Low-pressure, specific care lets them feel supported without having to do anything.

steps.prompt: Take the pressure off.
steps.before: Thinking of you. No need to
steps.why: Telling them they don’t have to respond makes your message a gift, not a task.

steps.prompt: Is there a friend going through something hard right now? What could you offer?
steps.placeholder: e.g. drop round dinner on Sunday

steps.prompt: Supporting a struggling friend. Put these in order.
steps.why: Small, steady contact with a concrete offer is easier to accept than a one-off “let me know if you need anything”.

steps.body: Send a no-reply-needed message to a friend who’s having a hard time.

lessons.title: Handle Different Opinions
lessons.summary: Disagreement does not have to become distance.

steps.title: Different isn’t a threat
steps.body: Good friends don’t have to agree on everything. Handling differences kindly can actually make a friendship feel safer and deeper.

steps.prompt: Planning a group holiday, you want a quiet cottage; your friend wants a busy city break. What’s the best approach?

options.text: Insist on the cottage; it was your idea first.
options.why: Getting your way might mean a resentful friend on holiday, which isn’t much of a break.

options.text: Ask what each of you most wants from the trip, then look for something that fits both.
options.why: Understanding what sits behind each choice often reveals options you hadn’t thought of.

options.text: Agree to the city, then grumble the whole time.
options.why: Going along with it then complaining tends to sour the trip for everyone.

steps.title: Needs behind wants
steps.body: “Quiet cottage” might really mean “I need rest.” “City break” might mean “I want adventure.” A lively town by the sea could give you both.

steps.prompt: Ask about their reason.
words: really expect me to give up
steps.why: Asking about their needs, not their position, opens up solutions you both feel good about.

steps.prompt: In a disagreement, is it helpful?

cards.text: “What matters most to you about it?”
Looking for an option you’d both enjoy

steps.why: Helpful moves stay curious and honest; unhelpful ones put the person down or hide what you really think.

steps.body: Next time you and a friend want different things, ask what they most want from it before deciding together.

lessons.title: Stay Curious
lessons.summary: Ask how they got there before you argue.

steps.title: Curiosity cools things down
steps.body: When a friend says something you strongly disagree with, the urge is to correct them. Asking how they came to that view first keeps the talk friendly, and you may learn something.

steps.prompt: Over dinner, a friend says they’ve stopped getting vaccines. You strongly disagree. What’s the best first response?

options.text: “That’s ridiculous.”
options.why: Dismissing them shuts the conversation down and puts them on the defensive.

options.text: “Oh, that’s a big change. What made you decide that?”
options.why: Curiosity keeps them talking, and you can share your view once you understand theirs.

options.text: Quietly change the subject and avoid it forever.
options.why: Sometimes fine, but always avoiding can leave a silent gap between you.

steps.prompt: A curious opener.
steps.before: I see it differently, but I’m
steps.why: Being honest that you disagree while staying curious keeps respect on both sides.

steps.prompt: Which topics make you lose your curiosity fastest?
steps.reply: Knowing your hot topics helps you take a breath before jumping in.

steps.prompt: Match each argument starter with a curious one.

pairs.b: “How did you get to that view?”

steps.why: Curious questions keep the door open, so a disagreement stays a conversation rather than a fight.

steps.body: Next time you disagree with a friend, ask one genuine question about their view before sharing yours.

lessons.title: Agree to Differ
lessons.summary: Some differences don’t need to be solved.

steps.title: Not every difference needs a winner
steps.body: Some disagreements, about politics, faith or how to raise kids, won’t be settled over coffee. Agreeing to differ, kindly, lets the friendship be bigger than the topic.

steps.prompt: You and a friend have debated the same political issue three times now, and it’s getting heated. What’s best?

options.text: Keep going until one of you admits they’re wrong.
options.why: Some debates have no finish line, and pushing can cost the friendship.

options.text: “We see this one differently, and that’s okay. Shall we park it?”
options.why: You name the difference with respect and choose the friendship over winning.

options.text: Stop seeing them.
options.why: One topic rarely needs to end a friendship that’s good in other ways.

steps.prompt: Park it kindly.
steps.why: Agreeing to differ respects both views and lets you move on together.

steps.prompt: Is there a topic you and a friend should agree to differ on?
steps.reply: Parking a topic isn’t avoiding. It’s choosing what matters most to you both.

steps.title: Round four

lines.text: Okay, but did you see that article I sent? It proves my point 😤
You HAVE to admit it now.

steps.prompt: You still disagree. Reply:

options.text: I see why it convinces you, but we see it differently. Pub quiz Friday instead? 😄
options.reaction: Haha fine. Yes to the quiz!
options.why: You acknowledge their view, hold yours and turn back to the friendship.

options.text: That article is complete rubbish.
options.why: It restarts the fight and makes them dig in harder.

options.text: Fine, you’re right.
options.why: Giving in when you don’t agree can leave you quietly resentful.

steps.body: If one topic keeps causing friction with a friend, suggest kindly that you agree to differ on it.

lessons.title: Group Chat Tension
lessons.summary: Take tricky talks out of the group.

steps.title: Group chats amplify tension
steps.body: In a group chat, everyone watches, nobody can see faces, and people take sides. A disagreement that would be a quick chat one-to-one can quickly turn public and messy.

steps.prompt: In the group chat, a friend makes a sarcastic dig about you always cancelling. Others go quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Fire back a sarcastic reply in the group.
options.why: It escalates in front of everyone and makes others pick sides.

options.text: Leave the group without a word.
options.why: Leaving raises questions and doesn’t sort out what’s really going on.

options.text: Message them privately: “Hey, that stung a bit. Have I been letting you down?”
options.why: Moving it to a private chat lets you both be honest without an audience.

steps.prompt: Move it somewhere better.
steps.why: Private chats lower the stakes, so people can listen instead of saving face.

steps.prompt: What do you usually do when the group chat gets tense?
steps.reply: There’s no single right move, but taking real issues private usually helps most.

steps.prompt: Calms the group chat, or heats it up?

cards.text: Taking sides in front of everyone

steps.why: Taking things private and in person calms them down; audiences, side-taking and sarcasm keep the fire going.

steps.body: If a group chat gets tense this week, take the real conversation one-to-one.

lessons.title: Repair a Misstep
lessons.summary: Small repairs protect big friendships.

steps.title: Jokes can land badly
steps.body: Teasing is part of many friendships, until it touches something painful. When a joke hurts, how you respond matters more than the joke itself.

steps.prompt: In front of others, you joked about your friend’s break-up, and their face fell. What’s the best next step?

options.text: Later, privately: “That joke crossed a line. I’m sorry, I won’t do it again.”
options.why: It owns the hurt, promises change and respects their privacy by talking one to one.

options.text: “Come on, it was only a joke.”
options.why: It tells them their hurt isn’t valid, which can sting more than the joke did.

options.text: Tell the group they’re being oversensitive.
options.why: Talking about them to others adds embarrassment and can damage trust in the group.

steps.prompt: Own it simply.
steps.why: A simple, sincere apology is all that’s needed, with no defending or minimising.

steps.prompt: What usually stops you apologising to a friend?
steps.reply: All very human. A short apology costs little and keeps the friendship strong.

steps.prompt: Put the parts of a good apology in order.
steps.why: Naming the action and its impact first shows you understand, so the sorry and the promise feel real.

steps.body: If you’ve hurt a friend recently, own it in a sentence or two, without defending yourself.

lessons.title: Raise a Hurt
lessons.summary: Tell a friend when something stung, gently.

steps.title: Hurts left unsaid turn into distance
steps.body: When a friend hurts you and you say nothing, you often pull away without them knowing why. Telling them gently gives the friendship a chance to heal.

steps.prompt: Your friend made a joke about your weight in front of others. It really hurt. What’s the best way to raise it?

options.text: Laugh it off and quietly see them less.
options.why: They never learn it hurt, and the friendship slowly fades.

options.text: “That joke about my weight hurt. I know you didn’t mean it, but please don’t again.”
options.why: Clear about the hurt, generous about their intent, and clear about what you need.

options.text: Make a joke about them next time to even it out.
options.why: Payback adds a second hurt instead of fixing the first.

steps.prompt: Assume good intent.
steps.why: Saying you trust their intentions makes it much easier for them to hear you.

steps.prompt: What usually stops you telling a friend they hurt you?
steps.reply: Good friends would rather know. A gentle word now saves a slow drift later.

steps.prompt: Raising a hurt. Put these in order.
items: Say what happened and how it felt
Ask for what you need next time
steps.why: Calm and privacy help them listen; naming the feeling and a clear ask turn a hurt into a fix.

steps.body: If a friend has hurt you recently, plan a calm, private moment to tell them how it felt.

lessons.title: Accept an Apology
lessons.summary: Letting a sorry land is part of repair too.

steps.title: Repair takes two people
steps.body: When a friend apologises, how you respond matters. Accepting it, even if you still feel a little sore, tells them it was worth saying sorry.

steps.prompt: Your friend sincerely apologises for missing your birthday. You’re still a bit hurt. What’s the best response?

options.text: “Fine, whatever.”
options.why: A cold reply makes them feel the apology didn’t matter.

options.text: “Thank you for saying that. It did sting, but I really appreciate it.”
options.why: You accept the apology and stay honest that it hurt, which closes the loop kindly.

options.text: “Well, you should be sorry.”
options.why: It turns the apology into a moment to punish rather than repair.

steps.prompt: Let the apology land.
steps.why: Thanking them for the apology encourages honesty between you in the future.

steps.prompt: How do you usually react when a friend apologises?
steps.reply: Noticing your reaction helps you make apologies feel safe to give.

steps.prompt: Match each cold reply with a warmer one.
steps.why: Warm replies let an apology do its job, while cold ones make it harder for either of you to say sorry next time.

steps.body: The next time a friend says sorry, thank them for it before saying anything else.

lessons.title: Break a Long Silence
lessons.summary: It’s never too late to send the first message.

steps.title: Awkwardness fades fast
steps.body: After months or years without contact, getting in touch can feel awkward. But most people are touched to hear from an old friend, and the awkwardness lasts about one message.

steps.prompt: You and a close friend drifted apart two years ago, with no falling-out. You miss them. What do you send?

options.text: “Saw a dog that looked just like Bruno and thought of you! How have you been? 💛”
options.why: A warm, light message with a shared memory makes it easy for them to reply.

options.text: A long message explaining why you drifted apart.
options.why: Too heavy for a first message. They may not know how to respond.

options.text: Nothing. It’s been too long now.
options.why: The longer the wait, the harder it feels, but it’s rarely too late.

steps.prompt: Keep the first message light.
steps.why: “Thinking of you” is warm and asks nothing of them except a reply.

steps.prompt: Is there an old friend you’d love to hear from?
steps.reply: You could be the person who goes first. It might make their week.

steps.title: Two years later

lines.text: Saw a dog just like Bruno today and thought of you! How are you? 💛
Oh wow, hi!! I’ve thought about messaging you so many times
Sorry I was so rubbish at keeping in touch 😅

steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: Yeah, you really were.
options.why: Blame makes them feel worse and can end the conversation.

options.text: Ha, we both were! I’m just so happy to hear from you. Coffee soon?
options.why: You share the responsibility lightly and move straight to reconnecting.

options.text: No worries. Anyway, bye!
options.why: It closes the door just as they opened it.

steps.body: Send a short, warm message to a friend you’ve lost touch with, mentioning a happy memory.

lessons.title: Make Space for Change
lessons.summary: Friendships can adapt to new life seasons.

steps.title: Friendships have seasons
steps.body: Moves, new jobs, relationships and children change how often friends can meet. A friendship can stay close even when its rhythm changes.

steps.prompt: Your best friend has moved to another city for work, and your weekly pub nights have stopped. What helps most?

options.text: Assume they’ve moved on and stop messaging.
options.why: They’re likely missing you too; silence can turn a change into an ending.

options.text: Insist they come back every weekend like before.
options.why: Expecting the old routine adds guilt to an already big change in their life.

options.text: Suggest a regular video call and plan a visit for later in the year.
options.why: A new rhythm that fits the distance keeps the friendship going instead of letting it drift.

steps.title: Low effort, high warmth
steps.body: A voice note on your walk, a shared playlist, watching the same film over a call. Small, easy rituals can keep long-distance friends close.

steps.prompt: Which friendship has changed rhythm, and what new ritual could suit it?
Match each life change with a way to stay close.
steps.why: The best way to stay close fits the friend’s new life, rather than asking them to fit the old routine.

steps.body: Suggest one low-effort way to stay connected with a friend whose life has changed.

lessons.title: Stay Close From Afar
lessons.summary: Distance changes the how, not the friendship.

steps.title: Long-distance friendships need a rhythm
steps.body: When a friend moves away, you lose the easy, unplanned meet-ups. Friendships that survive distance usually have a simple rhythm: a regular call, a shared show, a yearly visit.

steps.prompt: Your best friend has moved abroad for work. What’s most likely to keep you close?

options.text: Message whenever you remember.
options.why: Good intentions, but busy weeks can turn into months.

options.text: Agree to talk every day.
options.why: Too ambitious for most lives, so it may fall apart and feel like failure.

options.text: Set up a video call on the first Sunday of every month.
options.why: A simple, regular rhythm is realistic and gives you both something to look forward to.

steps.prompt: Small and regular wins.
steps.before: A short call every month beats a long call once a
steps.why: Steady, small contact keeps you part of each other’s everyday lives.

steps.prompt: Which long-distance habit sounds most doable for you?
steps.reply: Pick one and try it for a couple of months. Small habits keep friendships alive.

steps.prompt: Keeps you close, or lets you drift?

cards.text: “We’ll catch up properly when you’re back”
Sending a photo that made you think of them
Planning a visit for next year

steps.why: Regular small contact and a shared plan keep you close; waiting for the perfect catch-up lets the gap grow.

steps.body: Suggest a simple regular catch-up to a friend who lives far away.

lessons.title: When They Fall in Love
lessons.summary: Make room for their partner, and keep room for you.

steps.title: New love can shift a friendship
steps.body: When a friend gets into a new relationship, you might see them less. It’s normal, and often temporary. Being happy for them, while gently saying you miss them, keeps you close.

steps.prompt: Since your friend started dating someone, they’ve cancelled on you twice. What’s the best approach?

options.text: “Clearly you’ve replaced me.”
options.why: It sounds like an accusation and makes them feel guilty, not closer.

options.text: “I’m so happy for you two! I miss our time though. Can we keep Thursday nights?”
options.why: You celebrate their happiness and ask for something specific to stay close.

options.text: Stop inviting them for a while.
options.why: Pulling away can make the drift permanent when it didn’t need to be.

steps.prompt: Ask, don’t accuse.
steps.after: you! Can we plan something just us?
steps.why: “I miss you” invites them back; blame pushes them away.

steps.prompt: How do you feel when a friend gets into a new relationship?
steps.reply: All of these are normal. Naming it kindly is better than hiding it or acting on it.

steps.prompt: Match each worry with a helpful step.

pairs.b: Tell them kindly you miss them

steps.why: Each worry has a small, kind action that helps you adapt instead of drifting apart.

steps.body: If a friend is in a new relationship, tell them you’re happy for them and suggest one plan, just you two.

lessons.title: Let Friendships Change
lessons.summary: Some friendships shrink, and that can be okay.

steps.title: Friendships have seasons
steps.body: Not every friendship stays the same size forever. Some become occasional, some grow closer later, and some quietly end. Accepting this can free you from guilt and resentment.

steps.prompt: An old friend and you now have very different lives and see each other once a year. It feels a bit sad. What’s the healthiest view?

options.text: “We’ve failed as friends.”
options.why: Friendships changing shape isn’t failure. It’s part of life.

options.text: “This friendship has a different shape now, and I can still value it.”
options.why: You accept the change while keeping the warmth, which leaves the door open.

options.text: Force weekly plans to get back to how it was.
options.why: Pushing can create pressure that neither of you really wants.

steps.prompt: A kinder way to see it.
steps.why: Seeing friendships as having seasons lets you honour them, even when they change.

steps.prompt: Is there a friendship that’s changed shape? What do you still value about it?
steps.placeholder: e.g. We still laugh like old times when we meet

steps.prompt: Making peace with a changing friendship. Put these in order.
steps.why: Naming the change and the feeling first makes room to choose your next step calmly, not out of guilt.

steps.body: Think of a friendship that’s changed, and send a short message valuing what it still is.

lessons.title: Ask Before Advising
lessons.summary: Support begins with understanding.

steps.title: Advice can wait
steps.body: When a friend shares a problem, our instinct is to fix it. But unasked-for advice can feel like “you’re doing it wrong”, even when it’s good advice.

steps.prompt: A friend vents about months of job hunting with no luck. What’s the most supportive response?

options.text: “That sounds so draining. Do you want ideas, or would a vent help more?”
options.why: It acknowledges the struggle and lets them choose the support they actually want.

options.text: Offer to rewrite their CV tonight.
options.why: Generous, but jumping straight to fixing can make them feel you think they’re failing.

options.text: “Maybe you’re just being too picky.”
options.why: It adds criticism when they’re already low, and they may stop sharing with you.

steps.prompt: Offer a choice of support.
steps.why: Giving them the choice respects that they know what they need right now.

steps.prompt: When a friend has a problem, what do you usually reach for?
steps.reply: Each has its moment. Asking first makes sure your support fits what they need.

steps.title: A hard night

lines.text: Jo and I broke up last night.
I keep going over everything in my head.

steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: Honestly, you’re better off without them.
options.why: Judging the ex can make them feel they have to defend it, instead of feeling heard.

options.text: I’m so sorry. Do you want to talk it through, or a distraction tonight?
options.reaction: Can you come over? Company would really help 💛
options.why: You meet the hurt first, then let them choose what kind of support they need.

options.text: Download the apps and get back out there!
options.why: Rushing to the next step skips past a loss they’re still feeling.

steps.body: Next time a friend shares a problem, ask whether they want ideas or a listening ear before offering anything.

lessons.title: Sit With Hard Feelings
lessons.summary: You don’t have to fix it to help.

steps.title: Presence before solutions
steps.body: When a friend is upset, the urge is to cheer them up or fix it. Often what helps most is letting them feel what they feel, with you beside them.

steps.prompt: Your friend says, crying, that they feel like a failure after not getting into their course. What’s the best response?

options.text: “That’s so painful after how hard you worked. I’m here.”
options.why: You name the feeling and stay with them, so they feel less alone in it.

options.text: “Don’t be silly, you’re not a failure!”
options.why: Kindly meant, but it argues with their feeling instead of hearing it.

options.text: “There are loads of other courses. Apply again next year.”
options.why: Solutions can wait. Right now they need to feel understood.

steps.prompt: Just be there.
steps.before: You don’t have to say anything. I’m
steps.why: Sometimes being there quietly says more than any advice could.

steps.prompt: When a friend is upset, what’s your instinct?
steps.reply: Every instinct comes from care. Leading with listening usually helps most.

steps.prompt: Sitting with it, or rushing past it?

cards.text: “Do you want to talk, or just company?”

steps.why: Sitting with a feeling accepts it. Rushing to the bright side can make people feel their pain isn’t welcome.

steps.body: Next time a friend is upset, say “That sounds really hard” before offering any advice.

lessons.title: Offer Practical Help
lessons.summary: Swap “let me know” for something specific.

steps.title: “Let me know” puts the work on them
steps.body: “Let me know if you need anything” is kind, but people rarely ask. A specific offer, like dinner on Tuesday or walking the dog, is much easier to accept.

steps.prompt: Your friend has just had surgery and is stuck at home for two weeks. Which offer is most helpful?

options.text: “Let me know if you need anything!”
options.why: Kind, but they have to think of something and ask, which is hard when you’re unwell.

options.text: “Shout if you’re bored.”
options.why: Friendly, but it doesn’t offer real help with the hard parts.

options.text: “I’m doing a shop on Saturday. Send me your list and I’ll drop it round.”
options.why: Specific and easy to say yes to, with no extra effort needed from them.

steps.prompt: Make it specific.
steps.why: A clear offer with a day attached is much easier to accept than a general one.

steps.prompt: Which kind of help are you best at giving?
steps.reply: Offering the help you’re good at makes it easy for you to give and for them to accept.

steps.prompt: Match each situation with a specific offer.
steps.why: Specific help fits their situation and takes the effort of asking off their shoulders.

steps.body: Replace one “let me know if you need anything” with a specific offer this week.

lessons.title: Support Through Grief
lessons.summary: Keep showing up long after the funeral.

steps.title: Grief doesn’t keep to a schedule
steps.body: Support often pours in around a death, then fades. But grief can be hardest weeks or months later. A friend who remembers then is a real gift.

steps.prompt: Your friend’s dad died three months ago. Everyone seems to have moved on. What helps?

options.text: Avoid mentioning him so you don’t upset them.
options.why: Silence can make them feel their dad has been forgotten.

options.text: “I was thinking about your dad today. How are you doing with it all?”
options.why: Saying his name and asking openly shows you remember and are still there.

options.text: “Are you feeling better now?”
options.why: It suggests grief should be over, which can make them feel rushed.

steps.prompt: It’s okay to say their name.
steps.before: Most grieving people are glad when you
steps.why: Hearing their loved one’s name shows that person still matters to others too.

steps.prompt: What feels hardest about supporting a grieving friend?
steps.reply: You don’t need perfect words. Showing up gently, again and again, is what counts.

steps.title: A hard anniversary

lines.text: Feels weird that life just carries on.

steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: At least she’s at peace now.
options.why: Comforting phrases can feel like they’re closing down the sadness.

options.text: Stay strong! 💪
options.why: It can make them feel they have to hide how they really feel.

options.text: I’m so sorry. Today must be so hard. Want to tell me about her? I’d love to hear.
options.why: You acknowledge the day and invite memories, which is often what grieving people want most.

steps.body: Put a reminder in your phone for a grieving friend’s hard dates, like birthdays and anniversaries.

lessons.title: Suggest More Help
lessons.summary: Know when a friend needs more than you can give.

steps.title: Friends aren’t therapists
steps.body: You can be a great support, but some struggles need professional help. Gently suggesting it isn’t pushing them away. It shows you take what they’re going through seriously.

steps.prompt: For months, your friend has been struggling to sleep, eat or enjoy anything. What’s the kindest step?

options.text: Keep listening and say nothing about getting help.
options.why: Your support matters, but they may need more than a friend can give.

options.text: “I care about you and I’m worried. Would you see your GP? I can help you book.”
options.why: You show care, name the worry and make the next step easier, without pressure.

options.text: “You need therapy.”
options.why: True or not, said bluntly it can feel like a judgement rather than care.

steps.prompt: Offer to help with the step.
steps.why: Practical support with the first step makes getting help much less daunting.

steps.prompt: Would you know where to point a friend for support?
steps.reply: Knowing one place to suggest, like a GP or a local helpline, makes it easier to help.

steps.prompt: Suggesting more help. Put these in order.
items: Offer to help them take it
steps.why: Calm timing and specific, caring words make the suggestion feel like support, not judgement.

steps.body: Find one place to point a struggling friend to, like a GP or helpline. If anyone is in danger, call emergency services.

lessons.title: Celebrate Each Other
lessons.summary: Friendship makes room for mutual joy.

steps.title: How you respond to good news
steps.body: How friends react to our good news can matter as much as how they support us in hard times. Real enthusiasm says, “Your joy is safe with me.”

steps.prompt: A friend shares that they got a promotion, while you’re feeling stuck in your own job. What’s the best response?

options.text: Change the subject to how stuck you feel.
options.why: Your feelings are valid, but switching topics can make them regret sharing the news.

options.text: Congratulate them warmly and ask about it, then process your own feelings later.
options.why: They get the celebration they deserve, and your feelings still get attention, just separately.

options.text: “Lucky you, must be nice.”
options.why: A jokey dig can leave them unsure whether you’re happy for them, and cool the friendship.

steps.title: Mixed feelings are normal
steps.body: It’s human to feel a twinge of envy when a friend succeeds. You can feel it and still celebrate them. The twinge is about you, not them.

steps.prompt: Celebrate specifically.
steps.why: Specific praise shows you notice their effort, which makes celebration feel genuine.

steps.prompt: Celebrating or deflating?

cards.text: Turning to your own bad week
Sending a card or a little treat

steps.why: Celebrating keeps the spotlight on their joy; deflating shrinks it, even when that isn’t what you meant.

steps.body: Send one friend a specific message celebrating something they’ve done recently, big or small.

lessons.title: Handle Envy Kindly
lessons.summary: Feeling envious is human. What you do with it matters.

steps.title: Envy is a normal feeling
steps.body: Feeling a twinge when a friend gets the promotion, partner or house you want is human. Noticing it, without letting it leak out as coldness, keeps the friendship safe.

steps.prompt: Your friend gets engaged while you’re going through a breakup. You feel happy and envious at once. What helps?

options.text: Act thrilled, then avoid them for weeks.
options.why: Avoidance confuses them and quietly damages the friendship.

options.text: Hint that it’s all a bit fast.
options.why: Little digs let envy leak out and spoil their happy moment.

options.text: Congratulate them warmly, and share your mixed feelings later with someone else you trust.
options.why: You celebrate them honestly and give your own feelings somewhere safe to go.

steps.prompt: Two things can be true.
steps.before: I can feel envious and still be
steps.why: Mixed feelings are normal. You don’t have to choose one to be a good friend.

steps.prompt: What tends to stir up envy for you?
steps.reply: Knowing your triggers helps you notice envy early and handle it kindly.

steps.prompt: Handling envy well, or letting it leak?

cards.text: Changing the subject whenever it comes up
Asking yourself what you want for you

steps.why: Handled well, envy can even point you to your own goals. Leaked, it hurts the friend and the friendship.

steps.body: If you notice envy towards a friend this week, write down what it tells you that you want.

lessons.title: Say Thank You
lessons.summary: Tell friends what they mean to you.

steps.title: Friends rarely hear it
steps.body: We thank partners and colleagues, but often assume friends just know they matter. Saying it out loud, specifically, is one of the most powerful things you can do.

steps.prompt: A friend has supported you through a tough year. Which message will mean the most?

options.text: “You’re the best ❤️”
options.why: Lovely, but general. They may not know what you really valued.

options.text: “Those Sunday walks when I was low kept me going. Thank you for being there.”
options.why: Specific thanks shows exactly what they did and why it mattered.

options.text: Nothing. They know.
options.why: They might, but hearing it can still mean a great deal.

steps.prompt: Name the specific thing.
steps.why: Naming the exact thing makes thanks feel real and memorable.

steps.prompt: Which friend would you like to thank, and for what exactly?
steps.placeholder: e.g. Jo, for driving me to the hospital

steps.prompt: Match each general thanks with a specific one.

pairs.b: “Thanks for the soup when I was ill.”
“I love how you make me laugh.”

steps.why: Specific appreciation tells your friend what they do that matters, so it lands much deeper.

steps.body: Send one friend a specific thank-you message today for something they’ve done for you.

lessons.title: Build Your Traditions
lessons.summary: Shared rituals become the story of your friendship.

steps.title: Traditions hold friendships together
steps.body: A yearly trip, a birthday breakfast, a silly film night. Traditions give you something to look forward to and become the memories you talk about for years.

steps.prompt: You and two friends always say you should do more together. What’s most likely to last?

options.text: A pancake breakfast on the first Saturday of every month.
options.why: Simple, regular and fun. Easy to keep going and something to look forward to.

options.text: An expensive holiday together every year.
options.why: Lovely if it works, but cost and planning can make it fall apart.

options.text: Just doing things when you all happen to be free.
options.why: With three busy diaries, “when we’re free” rarely comes.

steps.prompt: What makes a tradition stick.
steps.before: The best traditions are simple and
steps.why: Repetition is what turns a nice plan into a tradition.

steps.prompt: Which tradition would you love to start with friends?
steps.reply: Suggest it this week. Someone has to go first, and friends are often waiting for it.

steps.title: Starting something

lines.text: Ugh, we haven’t all been together since March 😭
We need to be better at this

steps.prompt: What do you send?

options.text: So true. We should!
options.why: Everyone agrees, but nothing changes without a plan.

options.text: New tradition: pizza at mine, first Friday of every month. Who’s in? 🍕
options.why: You turn a shared wish into a simple, regular plan that’s easy to say yes to.

options.text: Well, I’m always free, it’s you lot who aren’t.
options.why: Blame makes people defensive instead of excited to meet up.

steps.body: Suggest one small, regular tradition to a friend or group of friends this week.
